cards.tip: WIN — Cole recognized the customer's repair fatigue and went straight to the comfort advisor: 'I'll call out my comfort advisor and they can come out and give you guys a replacement cost,' which earned the appointment.

WIN — Said 'I'll send over all the information to him, let him know what else is going on with the system and see what decision makes best for y'all moving forward' when the family explained David (with power-of-attorney) was the final decision-maker — your clarity on the process and who you'd be reporting to earned their trust to move forward with the full evaluation.

FIX — When you said "you'll need to get a new compressor," that was your moment to reconnect to their cost concern (wife asking about service cost, prior $12K repair) before diving into the R22 freon explanation—ask "Before I dig into the technical details, are you looking to move forward or want to understand your options first?" That acknowledges the weight and keeps them engaged.

FIX — When the customer asked how to test the compressor, ask 'Do you want to try the $1,227 fan motor and risk the compressor failing, or replace the whole system now?' to move him from discussing options toward a decision instead of walking away to think about it.

FIX — when presenting the downstairs AC repair, lead with what you found (unit failure), reconnect it directly to the customer's pain (the hot master bedroom), then present the solution and ask for approval.

FIX — When you discovered the wasp obstacle on the outdoor unit, acknowledge it to the customer before stepping away to call the office: 'There's wasps out there, but let me check with the office on how we can handle that' — that keeps them engaged in the evaluation instead of leaving them mid-inspection while you troubleshoot.
WIN — When the customer hesitated on scheduling work, you reframed the specialist visit as free information with no commitment—that objection turnaround sealed the TGL.

FIX — When the customer said 'this sounds expensive,' present two options (maintenance plan vs. replacement timeline) instead of just 'I'll write it up.' That price objection was the moment to build the decision.

WIN — Mario reframed the customer's frustration with repeated failures as a systems issue ('builder grade units just wear down'), not tech failure. That honesty + empathy built trust that moved the customer from skeptical to: 'I give you guys credit.' Next call: add a scheduled next step instead of just 'paper + review.'

FIX — When customer asked 'do I even do anything with that primary,' reconnect to their cost concern by either showing the immediate risk (potential water damage) or proposing lower-cost interim steps, rather than deferring to pricing; that was the moment to build the case for acting now.
WIN — Sold the premium filter option by leading with value (6-month durability, better filtration) and backing it up by negotiating a discount. Value-first framing beats price-first every time.
WIN — Led with warmth and crystal-clear boundaries about approval, positioning the customer to trust any additional work you discover in the inspection.
FIX — Customer in active home sale process with inspection tomorrow; timing eliminated close possibility. System damage ($3K damper, failing compressor) now seller's liability problem.
FIX — Call incomplete; assessment phase ends before decision conversation. Cannot evaluate sales effectiveness from this segment.
FIX — Transcript cuts off after greeting; insufficient data to evaluate full call quality and decision-making.

WIN — Overcame $6,700 repair sticker shock by pivoting to Option C (full system replacement quote): 'I can get someone out here to go over that information with you.' Customer shifted from rejection to agreement on comfort advisor appointment.

WIN — Used detailed technical teaching (ice buildup, R22 illegality, compressor amp readings) to build credibility, then offered Option C when customer resisted $6,700-$8,000 cost: 'I can get someone out here.' Turned objection into appointment.
FIX — Transcript ends as call begins; just starting maintenance inspection. Cannot evaluate tech's full diagnostic and sales approach from this opening segment.
FIX — Call ends mid-diagnosis during assessment phase. Incomplete recording prevents evaluation of decision-making and objection handling abilities.
FIX — When customer said he'd be happy to have work done, should have presented repair options to secure approval before continuing inspection.

FIX — When the customer mentioned the upstairs bedrooms were unusable overnight, that was the moment to transition to options, but the tech stopped at diagnosis without presenting a path forward or scheduling a follow-up.

FIX — When the customer said 'I'm not opposed to replacing the whole system,' that was your window. You diagnosed perfectly (compressor failing, parts obsolete), but you didn't present the Option C appointment. Should've said: 'Based on this, I'd recommend a Comfort Advisor consultation on a replacement system now, so you're not caught mid-summer. Can I schedule that for tomorrow?' That closes the deal.

FIX — Customer expressed frustration they couldn't safely upgrade the thermostat due to wiring complexity; tech explained the problem but missed reconnecting to solve it—should have said 'Once I identify your system type, I'll make sure we get that thermostat upgrade wired correctly' to move from diagnosis into options and toward a close.

FIX — When customer expressed concerns about future replacement timing and costs, ask clarifying questions about scheduling fall pre-sale inspection or registering units today; converting education into concrete booking would have flipped this into a TGL.

FIX — Present concrete upgrade options during the inspection walk-thru rather than deferring all to a future report; connecting findings to customer's peace-of-mind concern would move decision forward during this visit.

WIN — Your education about the January 2025 refrigerant regulation change and consequences was excellent, but close it: when customers understand the future risk, ask 'Should I put together an estimate for a proactive replacement so you're ready?'

FIX — After diagnosing comfort issues, present specific upgrade options (duct balancing, zoning adjustments) or schedule follow-up; staying in diagnosis mode misses opportunity to move customer toward decision.

FIX — The customer showed interest in managing the info at their own pace, but without presenting clear options or a defined next step (Option C or Comfort Advisor appointment), the diagnostic call ended without a path to close.

FIX — Despite strong empathy and excellent diagnostic setup, the customer's urgent personal situation (husband and daughter's medical crises) wasn't leveraged to frame an immediate Option C as peace of mind they need now.

FIX — Customer stated he wanted the system "topped off" or "evacuated and properly recharged"—his core need. Bradley correctly identified that EPA rules required a leak search first to confirm no leak, but never offered "leak search + full recharge" as an explicit, priced option that directly answered the request. Should have said: "Here's how we handle this within EPA rules: we do a leak search first, and if it's clear, we evacuate and put a fresh 13-pound charge in—that's exactly what you asked for, and it costs $X." Instead, he presented three unrelated options (repairs, future compressor, replacement), missing the reconnection moment and the direct option that would have landed the work.
FIX — Redirect personal chat after initial rapport; every minute spent on customer's life story is momentum lost toward closing the work order.

WIN — When the customer said they'd postpone the repairs, you said 'I would hate to see you put in $1,000 even... the compressor goes out, you're talking about 4,000 bucks... the heart of the system.' By anchoring the conversation to future pain instead of present cost, you created room for the specialist estimate option, and the customer committed to contact the company.
FIX — Dirty coils found with engaged customer is your moment; offer Option C for efficiency assessment and replacement evaluation before they leave.

FIX — When the customer said 'it ain't coming on. Something's wrong,' ask diagnostic questions—when it started, what happens now—before moving to the attic inspection; this assessment move shows you're diagnosing FOR them, not just gathering pieces of the story.
FIX — Deepen discovery during assessment: probe system age, comfort issues, maintenance history to surface needs before recommendations.
FIX — Reconnect to compressor caution reading and water damage risk when customer mentions getting quotes, then lock in a Comfort Advisor appointment before they leave.

FIX — When customer mentioned a prior motor start device repair, Bradley should have asked a follow-up check-in like 'How's the system running day-to-day — any comfort concerns?' to uncover needs that justify a future efficiency consultation. Personal rapport was strong, but conversation pivoted away from assessment to off-topic discussion, missing groundwork for Option C.

FIX — When customer discussed leak repair cost, frame the decision path: 'Your choices are quick-charge (won't stick without fixing leak), full replacement, or Option C where a specialist breaks down exact pricing and financing. Let me check one more thing and we'll map out which makes sense for you.'
FIX — When customer deferred to family, should have presented urgent recommended action with consequences and secured commitment before leaving.
FIX — When customer couldn't access units for full maintenance, offer to reschedule for complete service or set up Option C with a specialist to coordinate access and handle everything.
WIN — Joe's honesty about the system becoming a money pit and waiving the service fee out of concern for the customer's pets built trust that opened the door to the replacement conversation.

FIX — When you mentioned the "$39 special" at the end, you didn't present it as a decision Barbara could make; next time, come back from inspection with: "Here's what I found, here are your options—we can handle this today for $39 or schedule later—which way works for you?" so she has a real choice to commit to.

WIN — Secured specialist appointment and authorization by leading with diagnostics (amp draws, oil leaks, age) instead of price. Customer understood the problem before considering replacement cost. That credibility is what converts to the quote call on Monday.

FIX — After diagnosing the burnt switch, reconnect to the customer's concern and explicitly outline next steps (specialist appointment or options conversation). The diagnosis was solid; the handoff to decision was missing.

FIX — Andrew nailed the diagnosis (old 2004 system, motor wear) but lost the thread at the decision moment; when he said 'running itself to the ground,' he should have asked 'Do you want this reliable?' and offered two paths: repair now vs. replacement with financing.
